== ostrich-benchmark-2026.md
# Ostrich 0.9 compression benchmark (project wiki, March 2026)

Ostrich compressed our sample of application text logs 4.1 times on average (zstd level 3: 3.2 times), at 410 MB/s
on one core.

Scope: the sample held 2,000 text log files, each under 1 MB. Binary payloads, files over 1 MB and multi-core runs
were not tested, so these numbers say nothing about them.

== ostrich-readme.md
# Ostrich

Ostrich is a dictionary compressor for small text records. It trains a dictionary per stream (`ostrich train`) and
needs the same dictionary to decompress.

final.result:
**Probably not, and the sources here can't show that it is.**

- **Wrong kind of data.** The README describes Ostrich as "a dictionary compressor for small text records." Your archives are protobuf binary frames, 40–300 MB per file.
- **The benchmark doesn't cover your case.** The 4.1× ratio (against 3.2× for zstd level 3) and the 410 MB/s speed come from text log files under 1 MB each. The benchmark says outright that it never tested binary data, files over 1 MB or multi-core runs.
- **Extra work to manage.** Ostrich trains a dictionary per stream, and you need that same dictionary to decompress. For archives you'd have to keep every dictionary for as long as you keep the files.

If you still want to consider it, run Ostrich against zstd on a few real nightly files first. Until then, zstd is the safer default.

I saved the README and benchmark findings, with their scope limits, to the memcue research shelf so a later session can reuse them.
